Set 1.text: You get a chance to spend a month working on a real-world project outside regular classes. Which project would you most want to take on?
options: Investigate why a local lake is becoming polluted and test possible solutions.
Build an AI or software solution that solves a practical problem for students.
Study a health-related problem and understand how it affects the human body.
Create a campaign, product concept, film, or visual experience around an issue you care about.
Develop a business idea, understand the customers, and work out how it could become successful.

Set 1.text: Imagine you have to choose one kind of college project. Which part of the work would you look forward to the most?
options: Forming a hypothesis, collecting evidence, and finding out whether your idea is correct.
Building a working system, prototype, or technical solution and improving it through testing.
Understanding people's experiences and using that understanding to help them.
Developing the concept, visual style, presentation, and overall experience.
Planning the resources, costs, people, and strategy needed to make the project successful.

Set 1.text: Your school gives students access to a well-equipped laboratory, technology lab, studio, and business simulation room. Which would you spend the most time in?
options: Laboratory — conducting experiments and investigating how things work.
Technology lab — coding, building systems, electronics, or robotics.
Studio — creating designs, videos, visual concepts, or digital experiences.
Business simulation — making decisions about money, customers, products, and growth.
Human development space — studying behaviour, communication, learning, or wellbeing.

Set 1.text: A university offers you a choice of one short internship. Which experience would you be most curious to try?
options: Work with researchers analysing data and testing a scientific idea.
Work with engineers or developers building and improving a product.
Observe professionals working with patients, students, or people who need support.
Work with a creative team developing content, designs, or a brand.
Work with a company team studying customers, markets, money, or business strategy.

Set 1.text: You notice that students in your school are struggling with career decisions. If you had to work on the problem, which part would interest you most?
options: Study available career paths, compare evidence, and identify patterns in students' interests.
Build a digital tool that helps students explore and compare career options.
Talk directly with students to understand their concerns and help them make decisions.
Design an engaging career exploration experience with visuals, stories, and interactive content.
Develop a structured career-planning program and work out how schools could implement it.

Set 1.text: You are given a problem with no single correct answer: "How can we reduce traffic around schools?" Which approach would you naturally prefer?
options: Collect traffic data, identify patterns, and test what causes congestion.
Design a smart traffic-management system using technology and sensors.
Talk to students, parents, drivers, and local authorities to understand their needs.
Create a campaign or communication strategy that encourages better travel habits.
Develop a practical implementation plan, estimate costs, and coordinate different stakeholders.

Set 1.text: Your school is running a large public event and you can take charge of one part of it. Which would you choose?
options: Build the rigging, the wiring and the power supply.
Build the registration website and a live dashboard for the day.
Organise the first-aid cover and make sure the crowd stays safe.
Recruit and brief the volunteers, and make sure nobody is left out.
Run the catering, the seating and how guests are looked after.

Set 1.text: A hospital wants to improve what it is like to be a patient there. Which part would you want to work on?
options: Follow the clinicians and understand the medical steps a patient goes through.
Build an app that shows live waiting times and appointment updates.
Talk to people and their families about what actually distresses them during a visit.
Fix the lifts, the ventilation and the equipment that keeps failing.
Improve the food, the comfort and the everyday hospitality of a long stay.

Set 1.text: You get a summer working with a professional sports team. Which role appeals most?
options: Work with the physiotherapists on injury recovery and rehabilitation.
Build the performance-tracking software the coaches use.
Coach the players and plan the training sessions.
Build and maintain the equipment, kit and training machines.
Run the outreach programme that reaches children from poorer schools.

Set 1.text: A new restaurant is opening and the owner asks for your help. Which part would you take on?
options: Develop the menu, the kitchen workflow and what the meal feels like to eat.
Install the extraction, the refrigeration and the gas systems.
Build the online ordering and delivery system.
Make sure the food is safe, hygienic and nutritionally sound.
Hire and train the staff, and make it a decent place to work.

Set 1.text: Your city wants more people to be physically active. Which approach would you want to lead?
options: Design and build safe cycling lanes and running routes.
Organise leagues, fitness events and community coaching.
Screen people for the health problems that stop them exercising.
Work with schools and neighbourhoods to reach the people being left out.
Build an app that tracks activity and rewards people for it.

Set 1.text: A travel company wants to grow. Which part of the problem interests you most?
options: Design the trips themselves and what guests experience day to day.
Rebuild the online booking platform so it stops losing bookings.
Keep the vehicles, boats and equipment maintained and safe.
Prepare travellers for altitude, heat and the illnesses they may meet.
Work with local communities so they benefit rather than being displaced.

Set 2.text: Which type of achievement would give you the greatest sense of satisfaction?
options: Discovering something through research that others had not noticed before.
Building something that works reliably and solves a difficult technical problem.
Helping someone improve their life, health, confidence, or abilities.
Creating something original that people find meaningful, useful, or beautiful.
Turning an idea into a successful project, organisation, product, or business.

Set 2.text: Suppose you are preparing for a college-level competition where teams must solve a complex problem. Which role would you most enjoy taking?
options: Analyse information carefully and develop an evidence-based explanation.
Build, test, or technically implement the proposed solution.
Understand the people affected by the problem and make the solution useful for them.
Develop the idea, presentation, visuals, and way the solution is experienced.
Decide priorities, manage the team, and develop the strategy for winning.

Set 2.text: You are asked to choose one elective for a year, with freedom to explore beyond your regular subjects. Which would you be most likely to choose?
options: A subject involving research, experiments, environment, or advanced scientific investigation.
Programming, AI, robotics, cybersecurity, or emerging technology.
Psychology, human behaviour, health, communication, or social development.
Design, filmmaking, architecture, visual communication, writing, or digital media.
Entrepreneurship, finance, economics, marketing, leadership, or business strategy.

Set 2.text: Imagine you are allowed to spend one full day following a professional at work. Which day would you be most excited about?
options: Following a scientist or researcher as they investigate a question and interpret findings.
Following an engineer or technology professional as they design, build, test, and improve something.
Following a doctor, psychologist, therapist, or other professional helping people.
Following a designer, architect, filmmaker, or creative professional through the process of creating something.
Following an entrepreneur, consultant, manager, or financial professional making business decisions.

Set 2.text: Your team has six months to develop something that could genuinely help people. Which part of the journey would you want to own?
options: Research the problem deeply, gather evidence, and determine whether the proposed solution works.
Develop the technology or physical product and keep improving it through testing.
Spend time with the intended users and understand whether the solution actually helps them.
Shape the product's design, communication, usability, and overall experience.
Build the plan for funding, marketing, partnerships, operations, and growth.

Set 2.text: When you think about the next 5–10 years, which kind of work environment sounds most naturally appealing to you?
options: A place where you investigate questions, analyse evidence, and keep learning new things.
A place where you solve technical problems, build systems, and work with new technologies.
A place where you work closely with people and see a direct impact on their lives.
A place where ideas, creativity, design, communication, and experimentation are part of everyday work.
A place where you make decisions, lead initiatives, work with markets, money, customers, or organisations.

Set 2.text: You are given a small budget to improve health in a rural district. What would you do first?
options: Run clinics and treat people directly.
Train local volunteers and organise the community around it.
Build the water supply and sanitation that stops people getting ill.
Set up a simple digital records system that works without reliable internet.
Start sports and fitness programmes so people are active in the first place.

Set 2.text: A hotel chain asks for your ideas. Which would you most want to work on?
options: How guests are looked after from the moment they arrive to the moment they leave.
Re-engineering the heating, water and power systems so it uses far less energy.
The app that handles check-in, keys and room service.
The spa and wellness side, and getting the health claims right.
Staff welfare, training and progression for people who rarely get either.

Set 2.text: You have a year to work on something that makes everyday life better. Which problem would you pick?
options: A physical product that solves a practical annoyance properly.
A piece of software that thousands of people would use every day.
A health condition that affects a great many people.
Something that is going wrong between people in your community.
A place people genuinely enjoy visiting - a cafe, a gym, a venue.

Set 2.text: Which of these achievements would you be proudest of?
options: The machine I built has run for ten years without failing.
The software I wrote handles a million people without breaking.
The treatment I helped develop is now standard practice.
The programme I ran changed things for my community.
People travel across the city to eat at the restaurant I opened.

Set 2.text: The school canteen is crowded, slow and the food is poor. Which part would you fix?
options: Rebuild the servery counter and replace the equipment that jams.
Build a pre-order app so the queue stops forming at all.
Rework the recipes so they are nutritionally sound.
Make sure the students who cannot afford it still eat properly.
Change what is cooked and how the room feels to sit in.

Set 2.text: A relief camp is set up after a flood. Where would you be most useful?
options: Getting shelter, clean water and power working.
Set up the digital register that tracks who is here and what they need.
Treating the injured and preventing disease spreading.
Sitting with families, finding the missing and calming the panic.
Running the kitchen and getting three meals a day to everybody.

Set 3.text: Your team receives a large amount of information about a problem. What would you naturally want to do first?
options: Look for patterns, evidence, and possible explanations.
Figure out how technology could process or solve the problem.
Understand how the problem is affecting the people involved.
Find a better way to present the information so people understand it.
Identify the opportunity, decide what matters most, and plan what to do next.

Set 3.text: You are given a chance to improve something students use every day. Which part would interest you most?
options: Find out scientifically why the current solution is not working well.
Build and test a better technical solution.
Talk to students and understand what they actually need.
Redesign the experience so it is more attractive and easier to use.
Work out how the improved solution could be launched and adopted widely.

Set 3.text: Which kind of challenge would keep you interested even if the answer took several attempts to find?
options: A difficult scientific question where you need evidence before reaching a conclusion.
A technical problem where you need to build, test, fail, and improve.
A human problem where different people may need different solutions.
A creative problem where there are many possible answers.
A strategic problem where you must balance risk, resources, and opportunity.

Set 3.text: Imagine your college gives you access to a mentor for an entire semester. Which mentor would you be most curious to learn from?
options: A researcher who investigates unanswered questions.
An engineer or technology professional who builds real products.
A professional who works directly with people's health, behaviour, or development.
A creative professional who turns ideas into designs, stories, or experiences.
An entrepreneur or business leader who builds and grows organisations.

Set 3.text: You are asked to explain why a new product failed after being launched. Which part would you most enjoy investigating?
options: Whether the evidence reveals an unexpected scientific or technical reason.
Whether there is a flaw in the technology or system.
Whether the product failed to solve a genuine human need.
Whether its design or communication failed to connect with users.
Whether the pricing, market, strategy, or business model was wrong.

Set 3.text: If you could choose one type of problem to work on for several months, which would you prefer?
options: Understanding how a natural or scientific phenomenon works.
Creating a machine, software system, or technological solution.
Improving people's health, learning, wellbeing, or quality of life.
Creating something original that changes how people experience an idea or product.
Building an idea into a viable organisation, service, or business.

Set 3.text: A care home for elderly residents asks for help. Which would you take on?
options: Fit safe flooring, handrails and lifts that actually work.
Install sensors and software that detect a fall immediately.
Manage the medication, mobility and daily health of residents.
Spend time with residents who have nobody visiting them.
Improve the meals, the outings and what there is to look forward to.

Set 3.text: Your school wants to cut the waste it produces. Which part would you lead?
options: Build the bins, the composting and the collection system.
Track what is thrown away with sensors and a dashboard.
Study what the waste is doing to health in the surrounding area.
Persuade students to actually change what they do.
Change what the canteen buys, cooks and serves.

Set 3.text: Your city is hosting a marathon. Which job would you want?
options: Build the timing gantries, barriers and road closures.
Build the timing, tracking and registration software.
Staff the medical stations along the route.
Coordinate two thousand volunteers and keep them looked after.
Look after the runners, the food and the finish-line festival.

Set 3.text: A new community centre is being built in your area. Which part interests you?
options: Designing and constructing the building itself.
The booking, membership and access systems.
The health clinic that will run inside it.
The programmes for people who are isolated or struggling.
The cafe, the gym and the events that make people want to come.

Set 3.text: A family friend runs a small hotel that is struggling. What would you offer to do?
options: Repair the building, the plumbing and the equipment.
Get them online with a booking system and a proper website.
Sort out food safety and the staff's health and injuries.
Sort out the staffing, the training and the way people are managed.
Rethink the rooms, the food and what staying there feels like.

Set 3.text: Your class is planning a long trip abroad. Which responsibility would you take?
options: Transport, luggage systems and everything that has to physically work.
The tracking app and the shared itinerary everyone uses.
Vaccinations, medical kits and what to do if someone falls ill.
Making it affordable so nobody is quietly left behind.
The itinerary, the food and what everyone will remember.

Set 4.text: When you encounter something you don't understand, what are you most likely to do?
options: Investigate it until you understand the underlying reason.
Try to build, test, or experiment with it yourself.
Ask people about their experiences and perspectives.
Explore different ways of representing or explaining it creatively.
Think about how the knowledge could be applied to solve a practical problem or opportunity.

Set 4.text: Which kind of feedback would make you most excited to continue working on a project?
options: "Your analysis uncovered something important."
"Your solution actually works."
"This genuinely helped someone."
"This is original and beautifully designed."
"This has real potential to grow."

Set 4.text: Your project team has limited time and resources. Which responsibility would you prefer?
options: Determine which questions need to be answered before moving forward.
Decide what can realistically be built and tested.
Make sure the solution works for the people who will use it.
Decide what the final experience should look and feel like.
Prioritise resources and create a strategy to achieve the biggest result.

Set 4.text: Which kind of uncertainty would you find most interesting rather than frustrating?
options: Not knowing the answer to a scientific question.
Not knowing whether a technical solution will work until you test it.
Not knowing exactly what people need until you understand them better.
Not knowing what creative direction will produce the strongest result.
Not knowing whether an idea will succeed in the market.

Set 4.text: You are part of a team where everyone has a different strength. Which role would you naturally gravitate toward?
options: The person who analyses evidence and challenges assumptions.
The person who builds and tests the solution.
The person who understands people and keeps the team connected to their needs.
The person who shapes the concept and communicates the idea.
The person who sets direction and coordinates the team toward an outcome.

Set 4.text: At the end of a successful project, which result would make you personally feel that your time was well spent?
options: "We discovered something we didn't know before."
"We built something that works."
"We made someone's life better."
"We created something people remember."
"We turned an idea into something sustainable and successful."

Set 4.text: Which kind of problem would hold your attention longest?
options: Something mechanical that has to work every single time.
Something digital that has to work for millions at once.
Something going wrong inside the human body.
Something going wrong between people.
Something about how a place feels to be in.

Set 4.text: Where would you rather spend a working day?
options: In a workshop or on a site, with tools and machines.
At a screen, writing software that runs.
In a clinic or a ward, with patients.
In a classroom or a community hall, with people who need something.
In a kitchen, a hotel or out on a field.

Set 4.text: Which club would you actually turn up to every week?
options: Robotics and workshop.
Coding and game development.
First aid and human biology.
Debate and community service.
The sports team or the culinary club.

Set 4.text: Which compliment would mean the most to you at work?
options: It works, and it has not broken once.
The software is fast, and it never goes down.
The patient recovered.
This community trusts you.
Everybody had a wonderful time.

Set 4.text: You are offered a month of work experience. Which would you pick?
options: A manufacturing plant.
A software company.
A hospital.
A school or an NGO.
A hotel or a sports club.

Set 4.text: Something in your neighbourhood is badly broken. Which would you most want to be the one to fix?
options: The road, the drainage and the street lighting.
The council website that nobody can use.
The clinic where people queue outside for hours.
The fact that newcomers are shut out of everything.
The park and the sports ground nobody looks after any more.

Set 1.text: You are given a project on a topic you know very little about. What would you most likely do?
options: Explore different sources until you understand the topic from different angles.
Make a clear plan and start with the required parts first.
Discuss the topic with others and exchange ideas.
Try an unusual approach that makes the project different from others.
Wait until you understand exactly what is expected before deciding how to proceed.

Set 1.text: You suddenly become interested in a subject outside your regular stream. What would you most likely do?
options: Start reading or watching material about it even if it is unrelated to your current subjects.
Look for a structured course or plan to learn it properly.
Find someone who already knows about it and discuss it with them.
Experiment with the subject yourself and see where your ideas take you.
Decide whether learning it is practical before investing much time.

Set 1.text: Your teacher says there is more than one correct way to complete an assignment. What appeals to you most?
options: Try a method you have never used before.
Choose the approach that is most organised and reliable.
Ask classmates what approaches they are considering.
Create something that is noticeably different from the usual submissions.
Follow a method you already know will work well.

Set 1.text: You are visiting a college campus and have an hour with no fixed schedule. What are you most likely to do?
options: Explore areas or facilities you were not originally planning to visit.
Check the schedule and make sure you cover the important places first.
Start talking to students and ask about their experiences.
Look for something unusual or interesting that most visitors might miss.
Spend the time researching the course or department you are seriously considering.

Set 1.text: Someone challenges an opinion you strongly hold. What are you most likely to do?
options: Become curious about why they see it differently.
Think through the evidence before changing your position.
Discuss the disagreement openly with them.
Consider whether their perspective reveals something you had not considered.
Prefer to stay with your original view unless there is strong evidence against it.

Set 1.text: You have an important exam three weeks away. How would you normally approach it?
options: Decide what to study each week and keep track of your progress.
Start with the topics you find most interesting.
Study with friends so you can keep each other motivated.
Try different study methods until you find one that works best for you.
Study more intensely as the exam gets closer.

Set 1.text: You have several assignments due in the same week. What are you most likely to do?
options: Prioritise them and decide when each one should be completed.
Work on whichever assignment interests you most first.
Discuss deadlines with friends and coordinate your work.
Move between tasks depending on what you feel like working on.
Focus on the most urgent task and handle the others later.

Set 1.text: You realise halfway through a project that you may not finish it on time. What would you do?
options: Rework the schedule and make sure the remaining tasks are completed.
Try a different approach that could make the project more interesting and efficient.
Ask teammates to help redistribute the work.
Continue experimenting until you find a better solution.
Stay calm and focus on completing the most important parts first.

Set 1.text: You receive detailed feedback saying several parts of your work need improvement. What is your first reaction?
options: Go through each point and make a plan to correct them.
Look for different ways to improve the work rather than simply fixing the errors.
Discuss the feedback with someone whose opinion you trust.
Feel interested in trying a completely different approach next time.
Take some time to process the criticism before deciding what to change.

Set 1.text: You have been working on a difficult subject for several days but your performance is not improving much. What would you most likely do?
options: Change your study strategy and continue working at it.
Explore a completely different way of understanding the subject.
Ask a teacher, friend, or senior for guidance.
Try applying the subject to something practical or interesting.
Take a break and return to it when you feel more prepared.

Set 2.text: You are asked to present your project to a large group of students. What would you most likely do?
options: Volunteer to present and enjoy explaining your work.
Present confidently after preparing thoroughly.
Feel comfortable if you can interact with the audience.
Prefer to contribute through the content or design rather than speaking.
Feel nervous initially but become comfortable once you start.

Set 2.text: You join a college preparation programme where you do not know anyone. What are you most likely to do?
options: Introduce yourself and start getting to know people.
Observe the group first and gradually join conversations.
Look for people with similar interests and start talking to them.
Focus on the programme and let relationships develop naturally.
Wait until someone approaches you before becoming involved.

Set 2.text: Your team needs someone to lead a presentation. What would you most likely do?
options: Volunteer if you feel you can help the team succeed.
Offer to prepare the content rather than lead the presentation.
Encourage another teammate who would enjoy leading it.
Suggest that everyone share the presentation equally.
Take the lead if nobody else is willing to do it.

Set 2.text: You attend a career event where professionals from different fields are available to speak with students. What would you most likely do?
options: Approach several professionals and ask them about their experiences.
Listen carefully and approach only the people relevant to your interests.
Ask questions during the sessions rather than speaking individually.
Explore unexpected career areas because something new may interest you.
Prefer to observe and collect information without approaching people directly.

Set 2.text: Your group discussion becomes quiet because nobody wants to start. What would you most likely do?
options: Start the discussion and get everyone involved.
Prepare your thoughts first and speak when you have something useful to add.
Ask others what they think and build the discussion from there.
Introduce a different perspective to get the conversation moving.
Wait for someone else to take the lead.

Set 2.text: A close friend is worried about an important decision about college or career. What would you most naturally do?
options: Listen carefully and help them think through what matters to them.
Give practical suggestions based on what you know.
Spend time with them so they don't feel alone.
Encourage them to consider possibilities they may not have thought about.
Help them create a clear list of options and next steps.

Set 2.text: During a group project, two teammates strongly disagree about how to proceed. What would you most likely do?
options: Help them understand each other's point of view and find common ground.
Suggest comparing both approaches against the project requirements.
Encourage everyone to discuss the disagreement openly.
Suggest combining the strongest parts of both ideas.
Let them resolve the disagreement themselves unless it affects your work.

Set 2.text: You notice that a classmate is struggling but has not asked anyone for help. What would you most likely do?
options: Check in with them and ask whether they need help.
Offer specific help if you know the topic well.
Encourage them to speak with a teacher or mentor.
Think of a different way to make the task easier for them.
Give them space unless they ask you directly.

Set 2.text: Your team receives criticism from another group about your project. How would you respond?
options: Listen to the criticism and see whether it can improve the project.
Check whether their criticism is supported by facts.
Discuss it with your team before deciding how to respond.
Look for a creative way to address the criticism.
Ignore it if you believe your team has done its work well.

Set 2.text: You have to work closely with someone whose working style is very different from yours. What would you most likely do?
options: Adjust your approach so you can work effectively together.
Agree on clear responsibilities and deadlines.
Spend some time understanding how they prefer to work.
Try combining both working styles to create something better.
Keep following your own method and focus on your responsibilities.

Set 3.text: You prepare seriously for an important exam but receive a result that is much lower than expected. What happens next?
options: Review what went wrong and make a plan for the next attempt.
Feel disappointed for a while but then return to your routine.
Talk to someone you trust about how you feel.
Try a completely different preparation strategy.
Worry about the result for some time before deciding what to do.

Set 3.text: You are about to enter an important interview or selection process. How do you usually feel?
options: Nervous, but able to focus on what I need to do.
Mostly confident because I prepared carefully.
Excited by the opportunity to meet new people.
Curious about the experience even if I am unsure how it will go.
Very worried about what could go wrong.

Set 3.text: Your project presentation suddenly develops a technical problem in front of everyone. What would you most likely do?
options: Stay composed and work out another way to continue.
Follow the backup plan you prepared.
Ask a teammate to help while you continue communicating with the audience.
Improvise a different way to present the idea.
Feel stressed but try to continue anyway.

Set 3.text: You have several important decisions to make about your future at the same time. What is your natural response?
options: Break the decisions into smaller parts and work through them calmly.
Research every option before deciding.
Talk to people you trust and hear their views.
Explore different possibilities without deciding immediately.
Feel overwhelmed until you can narrow the choices down.

Set 3.text: You are selected for an opportunity that is more challenging than anything you have done before. What is your first thought?
options: "I'll figure out what I need to learn and prepare."
"This could be a chance to discover something new about myself."
"I'm excited to meet people and work with them."
"I want to try something ambitious even if I might fail."
"I need to understand exactly what could go wrong first."

Set 3.text: You have an important goal for the next year, but there is no fixed deadline. What would you most likely do?
options: Create milestones so you can measure your progress.
Keep exploring different ways of reaching the goal.
Share the goal with others so they can keep you motivated.
Set an ambitious target and experiment as you go.
Wait until you have a clearer reason or deadline to act.

Set 3.text: A teammate makes a mistake that affects the whole group's result. What would you most likely do?
options: Focus on fixing the problem first rather than blaming anyone.
Explain what happened and make sure it does not happen again.
Talk to the teammate privately and understand what happened.
Look for a different approach that prevents the same problem.
Feel frustrated but continue with your own responsibilities.

Set 3.text: You are offered two opportunities: one is familiar and safe, while the other is unfamiliar but could teach you something valuable. Which sounds more like you?
options: Choose the unfamiliar one if it gives me a chance to learn and grow.
Choose the familiar one if it fits my goals better.
Ask people who have tried both before deciding.
Choose the unfamiliar one because I enjoy new experiences.
Compare the risks and benefits carefully before deciding.

Set 3.text: Imagine your first year of college does not go exactly as you expected. What would you most likely do?
options: Adjust your plan and work out what needs to change.
Explore other subjects, activities, or paths that might suit you better.
Talk with seniors, teachers, or friends about your experience.
Treat it as a chance to try something completely different.
Feel discouraged initially but gradually get back on track.

Set 3.text: If your friends described you at your best, which description would you most want them to choose?
options: "Reliable — if they say they'll do something, they do it."
"Curious — they are always learning or exploring something new."
"Positive — they bring energy and confidence to the group."
"Supportive — they notice when others need help."
"Calm — they handle pressure without easily losing control."

Set 1.text: You are given a project with very little guidance and a deadline several weeks away. What do you naturally do first?
options: Break the problem down and figure out what information is needed.
Think of an interesting way to make the project different from others.
Find resources or people who can help you learn what you need.
Decide the tasks, deadlines and start working on them.
Bring the team together and decide how everyone should contribute.

Set 1.text: Your team discovers that the original idea for a competition project is not working. What would you most likely do?
options: Find exactly where the idea is failing and why.
Come up with a completely different concept.
Study how similar projects have solved the problem.
Change the plan quickly and continue working.
Get the team together and decide the new direction.

Set 1.text: You have to learn a topic that is not covered properly in your textbooks. What would you prefer to do?
options: Break the topic into smaller concepts and understand how they connect.
Find an unusual or visual way to understand it.
Explore lectures, articles, videos, books or experts until it makes sense.
Try different methods until one works for you.
Discuss it with others and learn through their explanations.

Set 1.text: You are responsible for completing an important group assignment while everyone has other commitments. What would you naturally take charge of?
options: Work out what information and decisions are needed.
Find a more interesting way to present the final work.
Help everyone understand what they need to learn or contribute.
Create the schedule and make sure the work gets completed.
Keep the group coordinated and motivated.

Set 1.text: You are asked to explain a complicated topic to students younger than you. What would you most likely do?
options: Organise the explanation logically from basic to advanced.
Use examples, stories or visuals to make it interesting.
Learn the topic more deeply before explaining it.
Prepare the explanation and practise it until it is clear.
Focus on understanding what the students are confused about.

Set 1.text: Your school gives you access to a new technology that you have never used before. What attracts you most?
options: Understanding how it works and what its limitations are.
Thinking about what new things could be created with it.
Learning how to use it properly and exploring its possibilities.
Trying it immediately and learning by doing.
Helping others understand and use it.

Set 1.text: You need to learn a difficult mathematical concept. What would you prefer?
options: Read worked examples and write the steps in your own words.
Have someone explain the reasoning behind the method.
See graphs, diagrams, or visual representations of the concept.
Solve several problems and learn through practice.

Set 2.text: You are learning a new topic in Biology. Which approach would you enjoy most?
options: Read about the topic and make structured notes.
Listen to a teacher explain how the concepts are connected.
Study labelled diagrams, animations, and illustrations.
Perform an experiment or observe the process practically.

Set 2.text: You have to remember a large amount of information for an exam. What would you naturally do?
options: Rewrite important information in your own words.
Read the information aloud or discuss it with someone.
Turn the information into charts, timelines, or diagrams.
Use questions, activities, or practice tests to reinforce it.

Set 2.text: Your teacher introduces a concept without giving many examples. What would help you most?
options: Read additional explanations and examples.
Ask the teacher to explain the concept in more detail.
Find a diagram, animation, or visual example.
Try applying the concept to a practical problem.

Set 3.text: You need to understand how a scientific process works. Which would you choose?
options: Read the process step-by-step from your study material.
Listen to someone explain what happens at each stage.
Look at an illustrated process or animation.
Perform or observe the process through an experiment.

Set 3.text: You are preparing for a chapter you have never studied before. How would you begin?
options: Read the chapter and highlight the important information.
Find a lecture or discuss the topic with someone.
Look for an overview video or concept map first.
Start solving examples and learn as you work through them.

Set 3.text: You are confused about a topic just before an exam. What would you prefer?
options: Read another explanation or reference material.
Ask someone to explain it to you.
Look for a visual explanation of the concept.
Solve a few questions to identify where you are getting stuck.

Set 4.text: You have to learn a new formula or method. What works best for you?
options: Write the formula and its steps several times.
Hear someone explain when and why the formula is used.
See the formula represented through a diagram or example.
Use the formula repeatedly while solving problems.

Set 4.text: You are preparing a school project on an unfamiliar topic. How would you prefer to research it?
options: Read articles, reports, and reference material.
Interview people or discuss the topic with knowledgeable people.
Watch documentaries, presentations, or visual explanations.
Visit places or collect information through practical observation.

Set 4.text: You are given a complicated topic with many connected ideas. What would help you understand it?
options: Write the ideas in an organised sequence.
Talk through the connections with someone.
Draw a concept map showing how the ideas connect.
Use examples or activities to see how the ideas work together.

Set 5.text: You are attending a workshop to learn something new. Which part would you enjoy most?
options: Receiving a handbook or written guide to follow later.
Listening to an expert explain the topic and answer questions.
Watching demonstrations and presentations.
Practising the skill yourself during the workshop.

Set 5.text: You need to learn how to use a new software or digital tool. What would you prefer?
options: Read the instructions or user guide.
Have someone explain how to use it.
Watch a step-by-step screen demonstration.
Open it yourself and learn by trying different features.

Set 5.text: You are learning a new language. Which approach feels most natural?
options: Read vocabulary, grammar rules, and written examples.
Practise by listening and having conversations.
Use images and visual associations to remember words.
Practise through activities, role-play, and real situations.

Set 6.text: You have to give a presentation on a difficult topic. How would you prepare?
options: Write the content and organise detailed notes.
Practise explaining the topic aloud.
Prepare slides with diagrams, images, and key visuals.
Rehearse the presentation several times and learn through doing.

Set 6.text: You are studying a chapter that contains many dates, events, or stages. What would you prefer?
options: Write the information as notes or summaries.
Discuss the sequence with someone.
Create a timeline or visual chart.
Use quizzes or activities to practise remembering the sequence.

Set 6.text: You are preparing for a competitive exam that includes unfamiliar question types. What would you prefer?
options: Read strategies and explanations for solving them.
Discuss different solving approaches with teachers or friends.
Watch demonstrations of how different questions are solved.
Attempt many questions and learn from your mistakes.

Set 7.text: You want to improve a skill you are currently weak at. How would you prefer to learn?
options: Read about the skill and follow written guidance.
Learn by talking to someone experienced in it.
Watch someone demonstrate the skill.
Practise repeatedly until you improve.

Set 7.text: You are learning how a machine or system works. Which would help you most?
options: Read a detailed explanation of how each part functions.
Listen to someone explain how the parts work together.
Study a labelled diagram or animation.
Handle, operate, or build something to understand it.

Set 7.text: Your teacher gives you a choice in how to learn an upcoming topic. Which option would you choose?
options: Read the chapter and prepare written notes.
Attend an interactive discussion or lecture.
Use videos, diagrams, and visual resources.
Learn through experiments, activities, or problem-solving.

Set 8.text: You are revising before an important test. Which activity feels most useful?
options: Rewriting important concepts in a concise form.
Teaching the concepts aloud to someone else.
Reviewing charts, diagrams, and visual summaries.
Taking practice tests and solving questions.

Set 8.text: You are trying to understand a real-world problem related to your subject. What would you prefer?
options: Read case studies and written explanations.
Discuss the problem with people who have different views.
Study graphs, images, or visual evidence.
Work on the problem yourself and test possible solutions.

Set 8.text: You are joining a new academic course or coaching programme. What would help you settle in fastest?
options: Receiving a clear syllabus, notes, and written instructions.
Having an orientation session where everything is explained.
Seeing the course structure through a visual roadmap.
Starting activities and learning how the course works through experience.

Set 9.text: You are trying to understand your strengths and areas for improvement as a student. What would you prefer?
options: Read a detailed written report about yourself.
Discuss your results with a teacher, counsellor, or mentor.
See your results through charts and visual profiles.
Try different study approaches and see what works best for you.

Set 9.text: You are exploring a possible career that you know very little about. How would you prefer to learn about it?
options: Read career guides, articles, and detailed information.
Talk to professionals, counsellors, or people working in that field.
Watch videos showing people doing the work.
Visit a workplace, attend an internship, or experience the work practically.

Set 9.text: You are learning about a historical event that has many causes and consequences. What would help most?
options: Read detailed explanations and write a structured summary.
Discuss why the event happened and its consequences.
Use timelines, maps, and visual representations.
Explore the event through activities, simulations, or role-play.

Set 10.text: You are preparing for an important entrance or scholarship exam. Which study method would you naturally rely on most?
options: Detailed notes, reference books, and written revision.
Study discussions, recorded explanations, or teaching someone else.
Visual summaries, diagrams, and concept maps.
Mock tests, timed practice, and solving large numbers of questions.

Set 10.text: You have learned a concept but want to check whether you truly understand it. What would you prefer?
options: Write an explanation of the concept in your own words.
Explain the concept aloud to someone else.
Draw or create a visual representation of it.
Apply it to a new problem or real situation.

Set 10.text: Imagine you have to learn something completely new on your own. Which approach feels most natural to you?
options: Find reliable written resources and work through them.
Find someone or something that can explain the topic to you.
Search for videos, diagrams, and visual demonstrations.
Start experimenting and learn through practice.

Set 1.text: You receive a lower score than you expected in an important exam. What would you most likely do first?
options: Review your mistakes and identify what affected your performance.
Feel disappointed but try to move on quickly without thinking much about it.
Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling.
Blame the difficulty of the paper or circumstances for the result.

Set 1.text: You have several important exams and deadlines approaching at the same time. How would you handle the pressure?
options: Identify what is making you stressed and plan how to deal with it.
Keep working continuously even when you feel overwhelmed.
Take a short break, regain focus, and then continue with a plan.
Avoid thinking about the deadlines until they become urgent.

Set 1.text: Your close friend becomes unusually quiet after receiving their exam results. What would you do?
options: Give them space unless they ask for help.
Ask what happened, listen to them, and respond based on how they feel.
Immediately tell them how they should improve next time.
Share your own experience so they know they are not alone.

Set 2.text: During a group project, another student strongly disagrees with your idea. What would you most likely do?
options: Explain your reasoning and listen to why they disagree.
Defend your idea until they accept it.
Let the group decide without getting involved further.
Try to understand both views and find a solution that works for the team.

Set 2.text: You had planned to prepare for an entrance exam, but your school suddenly changes an important schedule. What would you do?
options: Adjust your preparation plan according to the new situation.
Feel frustrated and continue following your original plan.
Look for another way to use the available time effectively.
Wait until the situation becomes clearer before doing anything.

Set 2.text: A teacher tells you that although you are capable, your recent performance has not been consistent. How would you respond?
options: Think about what may be affecting your performance.
Feel that the teacher does not understand your situation.
Ask the teacher for specific feedback on what you can improve.
Accept the feedback but continue exactly as before.

Set 3.text: You are extremely nervous before an important presentation. What would you most likely do?
options: Recognise that you are nervous and use a technique that helps you calm down.
Try not to think about the nervousness and simply start presenting.
Practise once more and focus on what you can control.
Avoid taking the lead and ask someone else to present.

Set 3.text: Your friend tells you that they are confused about their career choice. How would you respond?
options: Tell them which career you think would suit them best.
Ask what they are confused about and listen before giving suggestions.
Share what you have researched and let them decide.
Tell them not to worry because they still have plenty of time.

Set 3.text: Your group project is falling behind because two members are not completing their work. What would you do?
options: Finish your own work and let the teacher handle the rest.
Confront them angrily about not doing their part.
Discuss the problem with them and find out what is preventing them from contributing.
Redistribute the work and agree on clear responsibilities and deadlines.

Set 4.text: You prepare seriously for a competition but do not qualify. What would you most likely do?
options: Take some time to process the disappointment and then identify what you can improve.
Decide that you are probably not good enough for that type of competition.
Ask for feedback and use it to prepare differently next time.
Move immediately to something else without thinking about the experience.

Set 4.text: You notice that you have been getting irritated with people more often during exam preparation. What would you most likely do?
options: Recognise that your stress may be affecting how you respond to others.
Assume people around you are simply becoming more irritating.
Take a break and identify what is causing the irritation.
Ignore it because exam pressure is normal.

Set 4.text: You receive criticism about your performance in front of your classmates. What would you most likely do?
options: Respond immediately because you feel embarrassed.
Stay composed and think about whether the feedback is useful.
Feel upset but avoid showing it.
Ask for specific examples so you understand what needs improvement.

Set 5.text: A classmate who usually performs well suddenly starts missing classes and seems withdrawn. What would you do?
options: Assume they are simply becoming less serious about studies.
Check in with them privately and ask if something is affecting them.
Tell a teacher immediately without speaking to them.
Give them space and wait for them to approach you.

Set 5.text: Your team has to make an important decision, but everyone has a different opinion. What would you do?
options: Push for your preferred option because someone has to decide.
Encourage everyone to explain their reasoning before deciding.
Let the most confident person make the decision.
Help the team compare the options and agree on a practical solution.

Set 5.text: You planned to take a particular entrance exam, but you realise later that your preparation strategy is not working. What would you do?
options: Continue with the same strategy because changing it may waste time.
Identify what is not working and change your preparation approach.
Feel discouraged and reduce your preparation.
Ask teachers or mentors for advice and create a revised plan.

Set 6.text: You are balancing schoolwork, entrance-exam preparation and personal commitments. You start feeling exhausted. What would you most likely do?
options: Recognise that you are overloaded and reorganise your priorities.
Keep adding more study hours because there is no time to slow down.
Take some time to recover and then continue with a realistic schedule.
Ignore the exhaustion until your work is completed.

Set 6.text: You are asked an unexpected question during a presentation and do not know the answer. What would you do?
options: Admit that you do not know and explain how you would find the answer.
Try to give an answer even if you are unsure.
Become visibly nervous and ask someone else to answer.
Pause, stay calm and respond with whatever relevant information you know.

Set 6.text: Your friend is upset because their parents do not support the career they want to pursue. What would you most likely do?
options: Tell them to ignore their parents and follow their own choice.
Listen to their concerns and help them think through the situation.
Explain what you think their parents should do.
Encourage them to discuss their interests and concerns calmly with their parents.

Set 7.text: A teammate takes credit for an idea that you originally suggested. How would you respond?
options: Confront them angrily in front of the team.
Say nothing even though you feel uncomfortable.
Speak to them privately and explain how you feel.
Clarify your contribution calmly when the team discusses the project.

Set 7.text: You do not get admission into your first-choice course or college. What would you most likely do?
options: Decide that your plans have failed completely.
Explore other courses or colleges that could still lead toward your goals.
Take some time to deal with the disappointment before deciding your next step.
Ask someone experienced to help you evaluate your alternatives.

Set 7.text: You notice that you feel confident in some subjects but anxious whenever you have to speak in front of others. What would you most likely do?
options: Recognise that public speaking makes you anxious and identify ways to improve.
Avoid situations where you have to speak publicly.
Assume that you are simply not a confident person.
Practise speaking gradually and observe whether your confidence improves.

Set 8.text: You are waiting for an important entrance-exam result and find yourself constantly checking for updates. What would you do?
options: Keep checking because knowing the result quickly will reduce your stress.
Accept that the result is outside your control and focus on what you can do now.
Distract yourself completely and avoid thinking about the result.
Talk to someone about your worries and then return to your normal activities.

Set 8.text: A new student joins your class and seems uncomfortable interacting with others. What would you do?
options: Give them time and let them adjust on their own.
Introduce yourself and include them in a conversation or activity.
Assume they prefer to be alone.
Ask another friendly student to help them feel comfortable.

Set 8.text: During a group discussion, one person keeps interrupting everyone else. What would you most likely do?
options: Interrupt them back so others get a chance to speak.
Ignore it and continue with your own contribution.
Politely suggest that everyone gets a chance to speak.
Wait until the discussion ends and complain about it later.

Set 9.text: You planned to study with a friend, but they cancel at the last minute. What would you do?
options: Feel irritated and stop studying for the day.
Adjust your plan and study independently.
Find another person to study with.
Use the time to revise a different topic or complete another task.

Set 9.text: You receive a lower score than you expected in an important exam. What would you most likely do first?
options: Review your mistakes and identify what affected your performance.
Feel disappointed but try to move on quickly without thinking much about it.
Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling.
Blame the difficulty of the paper or circumstances for the result.

Set 9.text: You have several important exams and deadlines approaching at the same time. How would you handle the pressure?
options: Identify what is making you stressed and plan how to deal with it.
Keep working continuously even when you feel overwhelmed.
Take a short break, regain focus, and then continue with a plan.
Avoid thinking about the deadlines until they become urgent.
